place.zh: 沉鼎观 · 外门后院 · 柴堆
place.en: Chending Temple · Behind the outer court · the woodpile

_weather: 「天上却起了一层薄云，月亮躲在云后头」

setup.zh: 九月十七，入门第九天。夜里，你照旧坐在外门后院的柴堆上：吹呴呼吸，吐故纳新。
setup.en: The seventeenth of the ninth month, your ninth day. At night you sit on the woodpile behind the outer court as always: blow and breathe out, draw and breathe in.

recap.zh: 九月十七夜里，你的气在身子里转了一个圈——一夜通了小周天。银月说：三道关，她替你凿了两道半。「你是漏勺。本王是补锅匠。」
recap.en: The night of the seventeenth, your qi went round your body in one circle — the small circuit, open in a single night. Yinyue said she had chiselled two and a half of the three gates for you. "You're a leaky ladle. I'm the tinker."

zh: 一股暖，顺着脊梁骨往上走——一节，一节。
en: A warmth climbs the spine — one joint, then the next.
"Three gates. I chiselled two and a half."

story.zh: 九月十七，入门第九天。那一夜月亮刚过了圆，天上却起了一层薄云，月亮躲在云后头，只透出一团毛茸茸的白。后院墙根底下有一垛柴，松木的，一股松油味，跟他家屋后那一垛没两样。小满照旧爬上去，盘腿坐好，把木牌从衣领里掏出来，贴着胸口放着，又从怀里摸出那根鹅毛，搁在鼻子底下。这是他娘在家里教的法子：一口气吐得又细又长，心里跟着心跳数，数到一百二十，鹅毛不动，才算过了这一关。离家前那一夜，他数到九十六——还差二十四。他闭上眼睛。
story.en: The seventeenth of the ninth month, his ninth day through the gate. That night the moon was just past full, but a thin layer of cloud had come up across the sky and the moon hid behind it, showing only a fuzzy white glow. At the foot of the back courtyard wall was a woodpile, pine, smelling of resin, no different from the one behind his house at home. Xiaoman climbed up as usual and sat cross-legged, took the wooden tablet out from his collar and laid it against his chest, then took the goose feather from his coat and held it under his nose. This was the method his mother had taught him at home: let a breath out thin and long, count heartbeats along with it, and only when you reached a hundred and twenty with the feather not stirring had you passed this gate. The night before he left home he had counted to ninety-six: twenty-four short. He shut his eyes.

exits.means: breathes as the scroll says, sinks the mind down
exits._rise: 入门 — the one rise left (2026-10-16): one night of 小周天 lifts him out of 零层 to 一层 (story DESIGN: 九月十七, 银月「你比本王算的，快了三天」; Hanli 2026-10-15). 零层 holds no 修为, so nothing is skipped; 一层 starts empty (the 40 it paid went with the rule: no story 修为) — the header's 修为 bar first stands here.

story.zh:
吸进第一口气，他便觉出不一样来。那口气是凉的，清的，像他家屋后那口井里刚打上来的水。这一回它没有散，它一直往下流，流进肚脐底下三寸，一个他从来不知道有的地方。干得像大旱年份的一块水田，冷冰冰的，裂着一道一道的口子。

第二口气渗进去，那块旱田润了一片。第三口，润了一大片。喝到半饱，底下忽然**暖了**。他还没来得及害怕，那股暖竟自己动了起来。

顺着脊梁骨的最底下一节，一节一节往上钻，像一条火做的小蛇。钻到后腰，撞上了一道门。可那小蛇撞上去，那门竟是开着的，门轴上还带着一点刚凿过的毛刺。钻到后背正中，又是一道门。也是开着的。钻到后脑勺，第三道门。这一道门，只开了一半。

那小蛇撞上去，撞了一下，没撞开，缩了回来。他咬紧了牙，心里却不知怎的，想起了他爹拉弓的样子——先看风，后看鹿。拉满了，不忙着松手。等风歇一口气。

他便不撞了。吸，沉，吐。一口，两口，三口。等到第九口气吐尽，后脑勺里那一下疼，忽然歇了一歇，像风停了一瞬——他一口气吸到底，那股暖跟着这口气，一头撞了上去。

只听得脑中「轰」的一声，他眼前一白。那股暖撞开了门，冲上头顶，落回肚脐底下，稳稳地停住了。恰好是一个圈。他睁开眼来。鼻子底下那根鹅毛，一动也没动。

一只半透明的小银狐从木牌里钻了出来，蹲在他膝盖上，道：「……通了？」小满结结巴巴地道：「通、通了！银月，我一夜就——就——」它道：「知道。本王算好的。」银月又打了个哈欠：「你以为这一年，你是白蹲的？」

「你背上那三道门，你自己撞，撞到三十岁也撞不开。」银月道，「所以本王睡在你心口，每天夜里趁你吐纳，替你一点一点地凿。」「尾闾，夹脊，玉枕。本王凿了两道半。最后那半道，得你自己撞。」银月道：「炼精生真气。凡间管这个，叫练气一层。」

他想起每天夜里吐纳完了，把木牌捧在手心里报账，报完了，木牌总是暖的。那是谁捂的？原来是她。过了好一阵，他才道：「……所以我不是天才。」银月道：「你是漏勺。本王是补锅匠。」

他这才看清了它。它比去年秋天钻进木牌那一夜还要薄。银月把脸扭开，道：「本王是妖王。凿几道门，算什么。」又低声道：「……就是要多睡几天。」

「不过，你比本王算的，快了三天。」小满问：「快三天是好事吗？」它看着他，看了好一会儿，道：「是好事。本王的事，你给本王藏好了。」话音未落，它已不见了。他小声道：「……你多睡几天。我不吵你。」
story.en:
With the first breath in, he felt something different. The breath was cool and clear, like water just drawn from the well behind his house. This time it didn't scatter. It kept flowing down, into a place three inches below his navel that he had never known he had. Dry as a paddy field in a year of drought, ice-cold, cracked open line after line.

The second breath soaked in, and a patch of the parched field grew damp. The third, a big patch. When it had drunk about half its fill, down at the bottom it suddenly **grew warm**. Before he even had time to be afraid, the warmth began to move on its own.

Starting at the very bottom joint of his spine, it burrowed upwards joint by joint like a little snake made of fire. It burrowed as far as the small of his back and ran into a gate. But when the little snake ran into it, the gate was open, and its hinges still had a few rough burrs on them as though they had just been chiselled. It burrowed up to the middle of his back: another gate. Open too. It burrowed up to the back of his head: the third gate. This gate was only half open.

The little snake hit it, hit it once, didn't get through, and shrank back. He clenched his teeth, but somehow, without knowing why, he thought of the way his father drew a bow: Watch the wind first, then the deer. Draw it full, and don't be in a hurry to let go. Wait for the wind to catch its breath.

So he stopped hitting. In, sink, out. One breath, two, three. When the ninth breath had gone all the way out, the ache in the back of his head suddenly paused, like the wind dropping for an instant — He drew a breath all the way down, and the warmth, riding that breath, hit the gate head-on.

There was a roar inside his head, and everything went white in front of his eyes. The warmth broke the gate open, rushed up to the crown of his head, back to below his navel, where it settled and stayed. A full circle, exactly. He opened his eyes. The goose feather under his nose hadn't stirred.

A little half-transparent silver fox crept out of the wooden tablet and crouched on his knee, and said, "...Through?" Xiaoman stammered, "Th-through! Yinyue, in one night I... I..." It said, "I know. This queen worked it out." Yinyue yawned again. "You think you sat out this year for nothing?"

"Those three gates on your back, if you hit them yourself, you could hit them until you're thirty and they wouldn't open," Yinyue said. "So this queen slept in your heart, and every night, while you were breathing out and in, chiselled away at them for you, a bit at a time." "Tailbone, Spine Pass, Jade Pillow. This queen chiselled two and a half. The last half you have to break yourself." Yinyue said, "Refining essence into true qi. Down among mortals they call it the first layer of Qi Condensation."

He thought of how every night, when he'd finished breathing, he held the tablet in his palm and gave his report, and when he finished the tablet was always warm. Who had warmed it? It was her. After a good while he said, "...So I'm not a genius." Yinyue said, "You're a leaky ladle. This queen is the tinker who mends it."

Only now did he see it properly. It was thinner than on that night last autumn when it had crept into the tablet. Yinyue turned its face away and said, "This queen is a queen of demons. What's chiselling a few gates?" After a while it said quietly, "...Just need to sleep a few more days."

"But you were three days quicker than this queen worked out." Xiaoman asked, "Is three days quicker a good thing?" It looked at him, looked a good while, and said, "It's a good thing. This queen's business: keep it well hidden for this queen." Before the words had died away, it was gone. He said quietly, "...Sleep a few more days. I won't make a noise."

story_full.zh:
吸进第一口气，他便觉出不一样来。

那口气是凉的，清的，像他家屋后那口井里刚打上来的水，从鼻子里进去，顺着喉咙往下流，一直流进肚子里。往常这口气流到肚脐，便散了，像一瓢水泼进沙地，渗得无影无踪。这一回它没有散，它一直往下流，流过胸口，流过肚脐，流进肚脐底下三寸，一个他从来不知道有的地方。他看不见那地方是什么样子，只觉得出来：那里干。

干得像大旱年份的一块水田，冷冰冰的，裂着一道一道的口子。那口凉气渗进去，那地方便「滋」的一声，像烧红的铁淬了水。他吓了一跳，差点睁开眼睛，却听见胸口的木牌里，有一个极轻极轻的声音，道：「……别动。」他便不动。

第二口气渗进去，那块旱田润了一片。第三口，润了一大片。第四口，第五口，第十口，像一场透雨落进裂了口的地里，一点一点地喝饱了，喝到半饱，底下忽然**暖了**。先是一点暖，像有人在那里点了一盏灯。那盏灯起先只有豆粒大，一明一暗，跟他家灶间那盏掐短了芯子的油灯一模一样；烧着烧着，越烧越旺，暖意一圈一圈地荡开去，荡到他的腰，荡到他的腿，荡到他的指头尖。他还没来得及害怕，那股暖竟自己动了起来。

它冲出小腹，往下一沉，绕到后头，顺着脊梁骨的最底下一节，一节一节往上钻，像一条火做的小蛇。钻到后腰，撞上了一道门——他觉出那是一道门，硬邦邦的，冷冰冰的，横在脊梁骨里。可那小蛇撞上去，那门竟是开着的，门轴上还带着一点刚凿过的毛刺，小蛇一扭身，便钻过去了。

钻到后背正中，又是一道门。也是开着的。

钻到后脑勺，第三道门。这一道门，只开了一半。

那小蛇撞上去，撞了一下，没撞开，缩了回来。小满只觉得后脑勺像给人拿木槌敲了一记，眼前金星乱冒，那股暖在后脑勺底下打着转，一下一下地撞，撞一下，他的头便疼一下，疼得他牙根发酸。他咬紧了牙，心里却不知怎的，想起了他爹拉弓的样子——

先看风，后看鹿。拉满了，不忙着松手。等风歇一口气。

他便不撞了。他让那股暖在门后头停着，停着，一口气吸进来，慢慢地沉下去，再慢慢地吐出来。吸，沉，吐。一口，两口，三口。等到第九口气吐尽，后脑勺里那一下疼，忽然歇了一歇，像风停了一瞬——

他一口气吸到底，那股暖跟着这口气，一头撞了上去。

只听得脑中「轰」的一声，他眼前一白，像大晴天里抬头看了一眼日头。那股暖撞开了门，冲上头顶，在头顶上打了个转，翻将过来，顺着额头、顺着鼻梁、顺着喉咙、顺着胸口一路往下，哗啦啦地，像一道开了闸的水渠，落回肚脐底下，稳稳地停住了。恰好是一个圈。他睁开眼来。鼻子底下那根鹅毛，一动也没动。他这才想起来，方才那一口一口的气，他一口也没顾上数——可他知道，每一口，都早过了一百二十。

天上还是那层薄云，柴堆还是那个柴堆，可看出去的东西，全都不一样了。院墙上每一道砖缝，他看得清清楚楚；墙根底下那只蛐蛐翅膀上的纹路，他看得清清楚楚；三间房外，孙二狗在梦里嘟囔「娘，我不吃糠」，他听得明明白白。他坐在柴堆上，大气也不敢出，生怕一喘气，这一切便又没了。

一只半透明的小银狐从木牌里钻了出来，蹲在他膝盖上。它打了个哈欠，眼皮耷拉着，一脸没睡够的模样，道：「……通了？」

小满结结巴巴地道：「通、通了！银月，我一夜就——就——」

它道：「知道。本王算好的。」

小满一怔：「……算好的？」

银月又打了个哈欠：「你以为这一年，你是白蹲的？」

「你背上那三道门，你自己撞，撞到三十岁也撞不开。」银月道，「所以本王睡在你心口，每天夜里趁你吐纳，替你一点一点地凿。」它抬起一只爪子，在他后腰、后背正中、后脑勺上，各点了一下：「尾闾，夹脊，玉枕。本王凿了两道半。最后那半道，得你自己撞——本王替你撞，你这辈子都不知道门是怎么开的。」小满张着嘴，半天才挤出一句：「……那我这，算是什么？」

银月道：「炼精生真气。凡间管这个，叫练气一层。」

他想起在家里那一冬，每天夜里坐在柴垛上吐纳，什么都没有，小腹底下一口枯井。他想起每天夜里吐纳完了，把木牌捧在手心里报账，报完了，木牌总是暖的。他以为那是他手心捂热的；可也有好些夜里，他一下都没碰它，它贴在胸口，照样是温的——那是谁捂的？原来是她。三百多个夜里，他坐在柴垛上，只道自己是一口枯井；原来一直有人在井底下，替他挖。褚先生说得对，山是神仙背走的；可神仙也得先看见，有人在挖。过了好一阵，他才道：「……所以我不是天才。」

银月道：「你是漏勺。本王是补锅匠。」

小满「噗」地笑出了声，笑到一半，却笑不下去了。他这才看清了它。它比去年秋天钻进木牌那一夜还要薄，今天月亮躲在云后头，只透下来一团毛茸茸的白，那点光竟也能从它身上透过去，透过它的身子，他看得见后头的柴堆，看得见柴堆上一根一根的松木。它那一条尾巴垂着，垂在他膝盖上，连尖儿都不翘了，尾根上那八道断口，颜色比去年深了。他道：「……那你呢？你凿了一年，你——」银月把脸扭开，道：「本王是妖王。凿几道门，算什么。」它望着院墙外头黑沉沉的山，过了一会儿，又低声道：「……就是要多睡几天。」

它又打了个哈欠，这回打得很长，打完了，眼睛已经合上了一半，道：「不过，你比本王算的，快了三天。」小满问：「快三天是好事吗？」它看着他，看了好一会儿，道：「是好事。本王的事，你给本王藏好了。」

话音未落，它已不见了。他小声道：「……你多睡几天。我不吵你。」
story_full.en:
With the first breath in, he felt something different.

The breath was cool and clear, like water just drawn from the well behind his house. It went in through his nose and flowed down his throat, all the way into his belly. Usually the breath flowed as far as his navel and scattered, like a ladle of water thrown on sand, soaking away without a trace. This time it didn't scatter. It kept flowing down, past his chest, past his navel, into a place three inches below his navel that he had never known he had. He couldn't see what the place looked like; he could only feel it: it was dry.

Dry as a paddy field in a year of drought, ice-cold, cracked open line after line. The cool breath soaked into it, and the place hissed like red-hot iron quenched in water. He jumped and almost opened his eyes, but from the wooden tablet at his chest he heard a very, very faint voice say, "...Don't move." So he didn't move.

The second breath soaked in, and a patch of the parched field grew damp. The third, a big patch. The fourth, the fifth, the tenth, like a soaking rain falling into cracked earth, drinking its fill little by little, and when it had drunk about half its fill, down at the bottom it suddenly **grew warm**. First a little warmth, as if someone had lit a lamp there. At first the lamp was only the size of a bean, flickering, exactly like the oil lamp with the trimmed-down wick in the kitchen at home; it burned and burned, brighter and brighter, and the warmth spread out ring after ring, out to his waist, out to his legs, out to his fingertips. Before he even had time to be afraid, the warmth began to move on its own.

It rushed out of his lower belly, sank down, went round to the back and, starting at the very bottom joint of his spine, burrowed upwards joint by joint like a little snake made of fire. It burrowed as far as the small of his back and ran into a gate. He could feel it was a gate, hard and cold, set across his spine. But when the little snake ran into it, the gate was open, and its hinges still had a few rough burrs on them as though they had just been chiselled. The little snake twisted and slipped through.

It burrowed up to the middle of his back: another gate. Open too.

It burrowed up to the back of his head: the third gate. This gate was only half open.

The little snake hit it, hit it once, didn't get through, and shrank back. Xiaoman felt as if someone had struck the back of his head with a wooden mallet. Stars burst in front of his eyes. The warmth went spinning under the back of his skull and hit, and hit, and every time it hit, his head ached, ached until his back teeth hurt. He clenched his teeth, but somehow, without knowing why, he thought of the way his father drew a bow:

Watch the wind first, then the deer. Draw it full, and don't be in a hurry to let go. Wait for the wind to catch its breath.

So he stopped hitting. He let the warmth stay behind the gate, stay there, while a breath came in, sank slowly down, and slowly went out again. In, sink, out. One breath, two, three. When the ninth breath had gone all the way out, the ache in the back of his head suddenly paused, like the wind dropping for an instant —

He drew a breath all the way down, and the warmth, riding that breath, hit the gate head-on.

There was a roar inside his head, and everything went white in front of his eyes, like looking straight up at the sun on a clear day. The warmth broke the gate open, rushed up to the crown of his head, turned once there, rolled over, and came down by way of his forehead, the bridge of his nose, his throat, his chest, pouring down like a channel with its sluice thrown open, back to below his navel, where it settled and stayed. A full circle, exactly. He opened his eyes. The goose feather under his nose hadn't stirred. Only then did he remember that he hadn't managed to count a single one of those breaths. But he knew that every one of them had gone well past a hundred and twenty.

The sky still had that thin cloud across it and the woodpile was still the woodpile, but everything he looked out at was different. Every crack between the bricks of the courtyard wall, he could see clearly; the lines on the wings of the cricket at the foot of the wall, he could see clearly; three houses away, Sun Ergou was mumbling in his sleep, "Ma, I don't want bran," and he could hear every word. He sat on the woodpile not daring to breathe, afraid that one breath would make it all go away again.

A little half-transparent silver fox crept out of the wooden tablet and crouched on his knee. It yawned, eyelids drooping, looking as though it hadn't had nearly enough sleep, and said, "...Through?"

Xiaoman stammered, "Th-through! Yinyue, in one night I... I..."

It said, "I know. This queen worked it out."

Xiaoman was taken aback. "...Worked it out?"

Yinyue yawned again. "You think you sat out this year for nothing?"

"Those three gates on your back, if you hit them yourself, you could hit them until you're thirty and they wouldn't open," Yinyue said. "So this queen slept in your heart, and every night, while you were breathing out and in, chiselled away at them for you, a bit at a time." It raised a paw and touched him once at the small of his back, once in the middle of his back, once at the back of his head. "Tailbone, Spine Pass, Jade Pillow. This queen chiselled two and a half. The last half you have to break yourself. If this queen broke it for you, you'd never know as long as you lived how a gate opens." Xiaoman's mouth hung open, and it was a long while before he squeezed out, "...So what am I now?"

Yinyue said, "Refining essence into true qi. Down among mortals they call it the first layer of Qi Condensation."

He thought of that winter at home, sitting on the woodpile every night breathing out and in, and nothing there, only a dry well below his belly. He thought of how every night, when he'd finished breathing, he held the tablet in his palm and gave his report, and when he finished the tablet was always warm. He had thought it was his palm warming it; but there had been plenty of nights when he never touched it at all, and it lay against his chest and was warm all the same. Who had warmed it? It was her. Three hundred-odd nights on the woodpile, he'd thought he was nothing but a dry well; all along someone had been at the bottom of the well, digging for him. Master Chu was right: the mountains were carried off by gods. But even gods have to see first that someone is digging. After a good while he said, "...So I'm not a genius."

Yinyue said, "You're a leaky ladle. This queen is the tinker who mends it."

Xiaoman snorted out a laugh, but halfway through the laugh he couldn't go on. Only now did he see it properly. It was thinner than on that night last autumn when it had crept into the tablet. Tonight the moon was hidden behind the cloud and let down only a fuzzy white glow, and even that little light went through it; through its body he could see the woodpile behind it, see the pine logs in it one by one. Its single tail hung down over his knee, not even its tip curling up, and the eight stumps at the root of it were darker than last year. He said, "...And you? You chiselled for a year, you..." Yinyue turned its face away and said, "This queen is a queen of demons. What's chiselling a few gates?" It looked out past the courtyard wall at the black mass of the mountain, and after a while said quietly, "...Just need to sleep a few more days."

It yawned again, a long one this time, and when it had finished its eyes were already half shut. It said, "But you were three days quicker than this queen worked out." Xiaoman asked, "Is three days quicker a good thing?" It looked at him, looked a good while, and said, "It's a good thing. This queen's business: keep it well hidden for this queen."

Before the words had died away, it was gone. He said quietly, "...Sleep a few more days. I won't make a noise."

refuse.zh: 那一口气还在门后头打转。——三关，你自己撞：一呼，一吸，等风歇一口气。
refuse.en: That breath is still circling behind the gate. — Break the Three Passes yourself: out, in, and wait for the wind to catch its breath.
